title: CN Traveller Names 27 Best Indian Restaurants in London as Spice Route Heats Up
excerpt: The new guide runs from two-Michelin-star Gymkhana to South Indian pub food in Islington — a map of how regional, specific and confident Indian cooking in London has become.
body:
• Condé Nast Traveller's latest London guide names 27 Indian restaurants, framing the capital's spice route as hotter than ever, from Michelin-starred rooms to no-frills midweek spots.
  • The top end of the list's world is Mayfair: Gymkhana holds two Michelin stars, and Quilon has held its star for coastal south-west Indian cooking since 2008.
  • For a first visit, the guides converge on Dishoom — the Bombay Irani-café group known for its house black daal and bacon naan rolls — as the easiest entry point.
  • Regional range is the theme: South Indian pub food at The Tamil Prince in Islington, Kerala coastal dishes at Quilon, and the JKS group's newer rooms such as BiBi and Ambassadors Clubhouse.

London's Indian restaurants are, in Condé Nast Traveller's latest assessment, stealing the culinary spotlight like never before. Its new guide names 27 of the best Indian restaurants in the capital, and its framing is the range: new openings introducing regional variations and fresh takes on traditional recipes, running from Michelin-starred celebrity favourites to no-frills restaurants built for midweek comfort food.

The Mayfair top end

The fine-dining pole of London Indian food sits in Mayfair. Gymkhana, the JKS Restaurants room inspired by the elite clubs of colonial India, holds two Michelin stars — the first London Indian restaurant to reach two, winning its first star within a year of opening in 2013 and its second in 2024, according to SquareMeal's guide. Its tandoori masala lamb chops are the dish other rooms are measured against. Nearby, BiBi, chef Chet Sharma's Mayfair restaurant named for his grandmothers, and Jamavar carry the same group's newer cooking, while Veeraswamy, the UK's oldest Indian restaurant, anchors the historic end of the scene.

Regional, not generic

What has changed in London is that "Indian" no longer means one menu. Quilon, near Buckingham Palace, has held a Michelin star since 2008 for the coastal food of south-west India — seafood-led Kerala cooking under chef Sriram Aylur, as Olive Magazine's November guide describes it. The Tamil Prince in Islington serves South Indian sharing plates — Chettinad lamb curry, channa bhatura, onion bhajis — in a revived Victorian pub. Trishna in Marylebone does South Indian coastal cooking, and Hoppers brought Sri Lankan and South Indian street formats to Soho and Marylebone. The newer openings the Traveller guide points to keep pushing the same direction: a region, a format, a point of view.

The crowd-pleasers

For most Londoners, the scene's centre of gravity is Dishoom, the group modelled on the Irani cafés of old Bombay, with rooms from Covent Garden to Canary Wharf. Its house black daal, cooked for 24 hours, and its breakfast bacon naan rolls are the dishes rival guides consistently name first, and its Permit Room offshoot in Notting Hill has become a list fixture of its own. Gunpowder, with a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and Kricket's small-plates rooms round out the casual end that the 27-strong list celebrates alongside the starred rooms.

Why it matters beyond London

London is where Indian food abroad first proved it could hold its own against any cuisine at the top table — two Michelin stars, a century-old dining room still trading, and pub kitchens serving Chettinad curry next to a pint. For diaspora readers visiting or living in the UK, the practical read of the new guide is simple: book the Mayfair rooms well ahead, treat Dishoom's queues as part of the ritual, and use the regional specialists — Quilon for Kerala seafood, The Tamil Prince for South Indian pub food — when the craving is specific.
